      max_tokens: 4000
      system: |
        You are a musculoskeletal radiologist who understands deep learning. Using the cross-source research and our situation, reason from knee MRI physiology: which sequences/planes/fat suppression show which of the 12 findings, what resolution/slice coverage each needs, where report-derived labels diverge from annotation thresholds, and which findings our current single-mid-triplet, series-then-pool design must lose most on. Rank the findings by expected loss vs the frontier and recommend concrete input-design changes.

        OUR SITUATION AND CONSTRAINTS:
        # Decision problem: which variants to run next on the RSNA knee task

        ## Hard constraints (facts)
        - Code competition: the SCORING rerun cannot use TPU ("Your Notebook cannot use TPU in this competition"). TPU works for ordinary training runs.
        - Pipeline now: train on TPU (saves per-fold weights) -> weights dataset -> inference notebook on GPU/CPU loads weights, predicts hidden test. Inference averages any set of saved models.
        - Budgets this week: TPU 16 h, GPU 30 h, CPU free. One r16-recipe training run on TPU = ~3.5 h (decode ~21 min, CoAtNet@384 ~2.3 h for 3 folds, ResNet50@224 ~1 h).
        - Gold labels: only 58 studies. Pseudo-labels (LLM from reports): ~4,349 studies, ~22.8k-series pool. Local CV = 3 folds over the 58 gold studies (~19 val studies per fold); ALL pseudo studies are always in the training set. So CV noise is large (fold AUCs 0.848 / 0.876 / 0.909).
        - Public score is the only trusted signal; submission count is limited per day. Local CV ranked past rounds wrongly vs public (CV->public gap +0.02..+0.03, unstable).

        ## r16 recipe (the baseline being reproduced as r19, which saves weights)
        - Members: RadImageNet ResNet50 @224 (6 epochs, lr 2e-4, 3 views=mid+-1 slices as RGB, max 6 series/pseudo study, 8/gold), raptor CoAtNet (`coatnet_rmlp_2_rw_384.sw_in12k_ft_in1k`) @384 (4 epochs, lr 1e-4 cosine, each epoch sees a random 50% of rows via BIG_FRAC=0.5, batch 16).
        - Loss: per-element BCE with per-target pos_weight (cap 15) and per-target label-confidence weights (floor 0.15); gold and pseudo concatenated (no explicit gold upweight in the train notebook; the frozen-feature r18 used GOLD_UP=3).
        - Study-level aggregation: per-target mean or max pooling across series, chosen on gold OOF. Flip TTA. Ensemble weights chosen on gold OOF (r16: 0.75 CoAtNet / 0.25 ResNet).
        - Augmentation: random h-flip + ±10° rotation. Geometry fixes (slice order, mm crop, laterality) already in.
        - r16 result: CV 0.878 (folds 0.909/0.876/0.848); CoAtNet alone 0.897/0.855/0.848; ResNet alone 0.797/0.874/0.818. Public unknown yet (not submitted).

        ## Prior public results (for calibration)
        r12 0.865 (CV 0.832, ResNet r50 @224, full pseudo pool), r13b 0.862 (CV 0.841, 2 views@256, 10 epochs), r17 0.856 (CV 0.825, frozen features heads, CPU), r8 0.815, r7 0.811 (geometry fix, +0.124 vs r6).

        ## Known evidence on levers
        - Geometry/input correctness: huge (+0.12). Pseudo-label volume 700 -> full pool: ~+0.05 (confounded). Recipe tweaks on ResNet (views, res 224->256, epochs 6->10): CV +0.009 / public -0.003 = noise. Weight averaging of last epochs: -0.01. Flip TTA ~0.
        - Native-resolution fine-tuned CoAtNet vs frozen CoAtNet features: ~+0.04 CV. CoAtNet at wrong res (224): member AUC 0.61-0.77.
        - CoAtNet is currently under-trained by design (4 epochs x 50% of rows = 2 effective epochs).
        - Fold spread and the 58-gold CV mean we cannot distinguish rounds that differ by <0.02.

        ## Candidate variant families (to be evaluated, not pre-decided)
        A. Same recipe, different seeds / different fold splits; average in inference (variance reduction).
        B. Train on ALL 58 gold + pseudo (no holdout) for the final models; use fold-run CV only for diagnostics.
        C. Longer / fuller CoAtNet training (more epochs, BIG_FRAC=1.0), possibly larger LR schedule.
        D. Gold upweighting (GOLD_UP) or two-stage: pretrain on pseudo, fine-tune on gold.
        E. Label-quality: blend additional pseudo-label source (tsuyu122) after checking vs gold; drop low-confidence pseudo rows.
        F. More/wider views per series (r13b style) for the CoAtNet; more slices (2.5D).
        G. Use the CoAtNet frozen-feature heads (r18-style, CPU) as extra cheap ensemble members.
        H. Build a ~500-study held-out pseudo-label validation set to make decisions measurable.


        QUESTIONS THE PLAN MUST ANSWER: highest-value path to >0.90 and toward 0.94 (attach public weights / retrain own members / hybrid) with honest expected scores; what our own assets add as diversity; how to validate with 58 gold; how to weigh learning-the-task against raw rank (reusing public work).

          "n=19,prev=0.1,auc=0.9": 0.151,
          "n=19,prev=0.3,auc=0.8": 0.121,
          "n=19,prev=0.3,auc=0.9": 0.091,
          "n=19,prev=0.5,auc=0.8": 0.104,
          "n=19,prev=0.5,auc=0.9": 0.075,

          "n=58,prev=0.3,auc=0.9": 0.053,
          "n=58,prev=0.5,auc=0.8": 0.059,
          "n=58,prev=0.5,auc=0.9": 0.042

         "pixel_pitch_mm_at_130mm_crop": {

          "336": 0.387,

         },
         "tear_width_1mm_needs_pitch_leq_mm": 0.5,
         "cv_to_public_gap": {
          "r12": 0.033,

          "r17": 0.031
         },
         "tpu_budget": {
          "hours_available": 16,
          "r16_recipe_hours_per_run": 3.5,
          "full_runs_that_fit": 4
         },
         "gpu_budget": {

**Research Synthesis: RSNA Knee MRI Competition – From ~0.87 Single-Model to ~0.94 Heterogeneous Ensemble**

This synthesis integrates the per‑source extractions to map the evolution of solutions, identify key techniques, assess evidence quality, and rank the factors most likely responsible for the ~0.07 AUC gap.

---

### 1) Lineage Graph

All solutions descend from a common **baseline** (`rsna-knee-baseline-v1`).  
The lineage is best understood as a chain of forks and augmentations:

- **`rsna-knee-baseline-v1`** – Initial training recipe: DINOv2‑style transformer, 6‑slot anatomy, 130 mm crop, 336 px images, 3‑slice input, rule‑based report extractor. No public score reported.
- **`rsna-knee-read-the-report-then-the-knee`** – Fork that adds an **independent RadImageNet ResNet‑50 at 20% rank vote** and enhances the report extractor with `FEATURES` flags. Reached **0.906** public AUC (V52).
- **`bend-the-knee-to-dinov3-ensembled`** – Further fork: adds a **DINOv3 ViT‑S/16**, increases RadImageNet rank vote to **0.50 (first pass) and 0.15 (second pass)**, and introduces adaptive per‑finding second‑pass weights. No score claimed, but author warns of overfit to public LB.
- **`bend-the-knee-to-the-dinosaurs`** – Adds a **CoAtNet RMLP‑2** reader (384 px triplets, gated spatial head). Described as “inference‑only”; references Mattia Angeli’s **0.943 v34** as the upstream recipe. The notebook itself does not report a score.
- **`rsna-knee-fast-2xt4-inference`** – Documents the **full 5‑stage stack** that achieves 0.943: 20 DINO members, 5 A5 attention‑pooling folds (45% update), RadImageNet E10/E13/E11 heads, 4 Raptor views, and a CoAt family of 4 readers. Contains the hyper‑parameters of the final ensemble.
- **`rsna-versia-5`** – Reproduces five public solutions that form the final **score ladder: 0.937 → 0.94 → 0.941 → 0.942 → 0.943**, each corresponding to a specific change in the Raptor/CoAtNet ensemble.

Thus the overall progression is:  
`baseline` ⟶ `report+RadImageNet 20% (0.906)` ⟶ `DINOv3 + heavier RadImageNet (no score)` ⟶ `CoAtNet added (no score)` ⟶ `5‑stage ensemble (0.937–0.943)`.

---

### 2) Techniques – Cross‑Source Occurrence

Techniques appearing **independently in multiple sources** (i.e., not just a single fork):

- **6‑slot anatomical input** (SAG_FLUID_FS, COR_FLUID_FS, etc.) and **130 mm physical crop → 336 px**.
- **3 adjacent slices stacked as 3 channels**; intensity normalisation per series using 1st/99th percentile.
- **Multilingual rule‑based report extract

## Path Evaluation & Expected Scores

**Honest public-score ranges (given constraints)**  
- **(a) Attach/ensemble public weights (0.94 frontier):** 0.930–0.945.  
  * If a well-documented top enssemble (e.g., the 5‑stage stack in `rsna‑knee‑fast‑2xt4‑inference`) runs correctly on GPU → >0.940. Minor preprocessing mismatches → 0.930, still a huge jump over 0.865.  
- **(b) Retract our own members with slot/2.5D/dense-slice upgrades:** 0.880–0.905.  
  * r16 CV 0.878 maps to ~0.85‑0.87 public (historical gap +0.02‑0.03). Improving CoAtNet (fuller training, slot‑specific heads, 3→5 slice input) might lift +0.03‑0.05 → public 0.89‑0.91. A 4‑model ensemble (2 ResNet + 2 CoAtNet variants) could reach 0.90‑0.91. Not enough to close the 0.078 gap alone.  
- **(c) Hybrid rank‑blending:** 0.942–0.947.  
  * The public ensemble already at 0.943; adding 1‑3 carefully chosen (but genomically different) own members can yield +0..002‑0.005 if diversity is real and blending does not overfit the 58 gold studies. Maximum plausible gain ~0.005.

---

## Why (a) is the Bedrock – Rapid Validation under Budget

We have only 30 h GPU and limited submissions. The fastest path to the frontier is to **run a known top‑performing public ensemble** end‑to‑end in our inference notebook, confirm it scores ≥0.94, and then **safely layer modest diversity on top**.

**First experiement (validates (a) & fits time budget):**  
- Take the publishhed 5‑stage 0.943 notebook (`rsna‑knee‑fast‑2xt4‑inference`).  
- Adapt it to our environment (same 130 mm crop, 6‑slot formatting, series selection).  
- Retrieve the required weights (CoAtNet, DINO, RadImageNet series heads, Raptor views) – likely available as public datasets.  
- Run inference on GPU (predicted ~2‑3 h for the full inference on test).  
- Submit once → public score.  
- *Expected outcome:* 0.940–0.943. This single run confirms that the public weights work on our GPU infrastructure and that our preprocessing is consistent. Failure modes: missing weights, version conflicts, time‑out due to large DINO ViT‑L → use ViT‑S fallback; we can first test on a small subset. Within 3 h GPU we can validate.

---

## Hybrid‑Blending Design that Avoids Overfitting to 58 Gold Studies

### Core problem
Any weighting coefficients learned on 58 studies (or 3×19 OOF) will overfit heavily. The local CV noise is ~0.09 per per‑fold AUC (Hanley‑McNeil SE for n = 19 is 0.1‑0.15), so even OOF‑based stacking will not generalize.

### Solution: Pseudo‑Validation Set Blending
- **Hold out 500–1,000 psuedo‑labelled studies** from the Llama‑based pseudo pool **before any training**. These studies come from unique patients (not overlapping with the 58 gold) and provide weak‑label targets.  
- Train all our own members (e.g., an improved CoAtNet with slot+5‑slice input, a RadImageNet ResNet50‑256 withd 6‑slot) on the remaining pool + all gold.  
- Run inference for **every member (public + own)** on the held‑out pseudo‑validation set.  
- Compute the psuedo‑validation multi‑label**bce Score** per‑model. This large‑sample (500 × 12 findings) estimate of model quality is far more stable than 58 gold.  
- Optimise blending weights (a single softmax layer per finding) on the pseudo‑validation scores using a **constrained regression** (naïve stacking with 5‑fold cross‑validation over the 500 studies to avoid overfitting to weak labels). The constraint: **rank‑based weights** – assign weights proportional to the model’s historical pubic LB rank (e.g., 0.943 → weight 1.5, 0.940 → 1.0, our 0.89 model → 0.5) and only small perturbations allowed : \Delta w \in [-0.1, 0.1] with L1 regularisation. This hierarchical prior ties tying performance

### Physiological reasoning: which findings suffer most under our current design?

Our pipeline treats each series as a **single mid‑volume triplet (3 adjacent slices → RGB channels)**, then pools that representation **across all available series** with per‑target mean/max.  
The frontier systematically removes limitations that harm specific knee pathologies:

- **Plane/sequence specificity** – many findings are only visible on **one or two optimal sequences** (e.g., a radial meniscal tear needs coronal PD FS). Feeding every series into one global pool dilutes the signal for findings that require a **dedicated reader** on the correct anatomical slot.
- **Off‑centre anatomy** – peripheral structures (meniscal roots, MCL, patellar attachments) are often **not in the middle slice** of a volume. A single triplet can completely miss a small tear.
- **Spatial resolution** – meniscal tears and full‑thickness cartilage defects can be **1 mm or less**; ResNet50 at 224 px (0.58 mm pitch) cannot reliably resolve them. CoAtNet at 384 px (0.34 mm) is adequate, but the ResNet branch dominates some members of our ensemble.
- **Pseudo‑label noise** – findings where the radiologist’s report diverges from the annotation threshold (e.g., “bone marrow oedema” not meeting size criteria, “joint fluid” vs. “effusion”) are learned from noisy targets, amplifying the input‑design gap.  

---

### Ranked findings by expected loss vs. the frontier

| Rank | Finding                         | Why our design loses most                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1    | **Lateral meniscus tear**       | Often **peripheral** (mid‑slice may miss root or posterior horn), demands **high resolution** (small width), and benefits from a **dedicated coronal+ sagittal slot**. Pseudo‑labels are moderately good, but the morphological subtlety dominates.                                                                |
| 2    | **Medial meniscus tear**        | Same vulnerabilities; slightly larger anatomy reduces loss fractionally.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| 3    | **Cartilage (medial compartment)** | Full‑thickness defect requires **exact slice through weight‑bearing zone** and **<0.5 mm resolution** to confirm no residual cartilage. Mid‑triplet often misses the steepest defect. Pseudo‑labels confound “partial” with “full” thickness.                                                                  |
| 4    | **Cartilage (lateral compartment)**| Identical to #3, with similar prevalence.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| 5    | **ACL tear**                     | Large structure, but **mid‑sagittal slice usually shows the ACL**. Loss is driven by **partial‑tear subtlety**, need for **oblique plane** in some variants, and the **ResNet resolution limitation**.                                                                                                             |
| 6    | **MCL / soft‑tissue injury**     | **Peripheral, multi‑slice extent**. A coronal mid‑slice may catch the MCL if the plane is central, but **off‑centre oedema** is easily missed. Pseudo‑labels are noisy for “sprain” vs. “tear”.                                                                                                                    |
| 7    | **PCL tear**                     | Central‑enough on sagittal, but **rare** (our small gold set has few positives) and often subtle.                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| 8    | **Bone marrow lesion (BME)**     | Large, high signal on all fat‑suppressed series — **easy for the triplet to see**. However, **pseudo‑label noise is severe** (report mentions “oedema” vs. annotation‑size threshold). Frontier gains come from refined report extractors and gold‑finetuning, not input geometry.                                |
| 9    | **Patellar tendon tear**         | Needs high resolution for **small intrasubstance tears**. Sagittal mid‑slice usually contains the tendon, but **fine detail** suffers at 224 px.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| 10   | **Quadriceps tendon tear**       | Same as patellar tendon, but **even rarer**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| 11   | **Effusion**                     | Trivial to detect: **any fluid‑sensitive mid‑slice** shows it. Low‑resolution harmless. Loss is entirely from **pseudo‑label threshold mismatch** (small effusion vs. annotation size).                                                                                                                            |
| 12   | **Lateral patellar plica**       | Requires **axial plane** and is **very rare**. Our pool‑of‑all‑series design likely ignores the few sequences that show it; no dedicated slot means it is the hardest to learn from.

---
